To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) water, chloride, and urea permeate through different pathways; (b) the water permeability coefficient is 1.8 X 10-2 cm/sec; (c) the chloride reflection coefficient is 0.98; and (d) urea permeation is 1,000 times faster than chloride permeation.
the unidirectional flux of water, urea and chloride across the red cell membrane are not influenced by solvent drag.
the effluxes of 3H2o and [14C]urea, but not [14C]chloride, were independent of the direction of water flow.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether water, urea and chloride move across the human erythrocyte membrane through the same or different pathways.
the effect of net volume flow across the red cell membrane on the unidirected efflux of water, chloride, and urea from human red cells.
the study of the transport of water and solutes across the red cell membrane, and in particular with the question of the existence of a separate water pathway.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the human red cell is a model system for the study of the mechanism of osmotic water flow, but that the mechanism is not yet understood.
water flow through pores and solute flux across nonporous pathways are functionally independent of one another.
the pathways for the permeants studied in this work are independent of the water flow pathway and of each other, and that the permeant fluxes are not affected by the direction of the water flow.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
water flow across the cell membrane is not associated with any significant drag of urea or chloride.
the permeability coefficients of water, urea (and other small molecules), and chloride ions are all independent of the direction of solvent flow and of the direction of net volume flow.
the unidirectional solute efflux is independent of net volume flow and is therefore not affected by solvent drag.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the unidirectional flux of water across the human red blood cell membrane is independent of the direction of net volume flow.
the efflux of water from the red cells is independent of the direction of water flow and of the direction of the net volume flow.
the diffusional efflux of urea is unaffected by solvent flow across the red cell membrane.
